metadata.file_name: 80. Peters et al. (2025). Text-Based Approaches to Item Difficulty Modeling in Large-Scale Assessments: A Systematic Review.pdf
metadata.title: Text-Based Approaches to Item Difficulty Modeling in Large-Scale Assessments: A Systematic Review

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This paper is a systematic review that synthesizes results across 37 articles (46 difficulty-prediction studies) rather than analyzing a single ILSA micro-dataset. Because no student-level assessment dataset is pooled or re-estimated here, there is no application of ILSA sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the review’s own analyses. The review’s quantitative synthesis uses count-based aggregation and descriptive statistics of reported performance metrics, so weighting is not part of the methodological pipeline. For future empirical work using ILSA micro-data, analysts should apply the official complex-survey weights provided by the data producer when estimating population-representative relationships and when reporting uncertainty for model performance.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a systematic review that does not fit predictive models to student-level ILSA plausible values (PVs) or report any PV-based scaling/estimation procedure. The review aggregates published outcomes (e.g., RMSE, MAE, Pearson r, R², accuracy) across heterogeneous studies that used different item difficulty parameters (CTT p-values, transformed p-values, IRT b parameters) rather than re-estimating PV-based achievement scores. Therefore, PV handling and missing-data handling are not applicable to the review’s own analysis, and missing-data handling is not reported as a review protocol detail.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Not applicable: the study is a systematic review. It screened 93 articles, excluded 17 after abstract/keywords screening and 52 after full-text screening using criteria including (1) not large-scale, (2) focused on text complexity/readability rather than item difficulty, (3) not automated prediction from item text, (4) review articles, and (5) difficulty parameter not estimated from human test-taker responses. It then coded 37 articles and treated each dataset/assessment difficulty-prediction task as a separate study, yielding 46 studies for synthesis.

data.outcome_summary: This systematic review synthesizes 37 articles (46 difficulty-prediction studies) on text-based item difficulty modeling in large-scale assessment contexts, focusing on models that predict item difficulty parameters from item text and related metadata. Across the reviewed studies, item difficulty was operationalized using CTT p-values and transformed p-values as well as IRT b-parameters (with regression framed as the dominant task), and performance was summarized using common metrics such as RMSE, MAE, MSE, R², and Pearson/Spearman correlations, plus accuracy metrics for categorical difficulty. The review reports benchmark ranges including RMSE as low as 0.165 and Pearson correlation as high as 0.87, with exact accuracy up to 0.806, while emphasizing that results are not directly comparable due to heterogeneity in datasets, difficulty parameter definitions, and evaluation protocols. Methodologically, the review highlights under-reporting of preprocessing and the need for standardized benchmarking, and it notes that many studies come from the BEA shared task (USMLE items), which may bias observed trends. Because this is not an original empirical ML study, no single weighting scheme, PV handling strategy, or missing-data procedure is estimated by the authors.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is a systematic review rather than an empirical ILSA micro-data analysis. As a result, there is no student-level sample, no country-level per-country N, no PV estimation/scaling step, and no ML model training/evaluation performed by the review itself; it only aggregates reported outcomes from included studies. Consequently, fields such as total_students, countries, and ml_techniques are intentionally left empty/null, and the methodological emphasis is on the review’s screening/coding and synthesis approach.
